explanations.explanation: Verse 4 says the book gives prudence to the simple, and knowledge and discretion to the young. Two groups, two gifts. I think it's good news for anybody still learning, because nobody has to walk in already knowing it all. I started out in a bin with a 25 cent sticker, so I'm very pro-beginner.

I checked verse 4 for a VIP section, baker. No velvet rope, no reserved seats. It names the simple and the young, and that's who gets prudence, knowledge and discretion. The rich and the powerful just aren't mentioned there.

Verse 4 never mentions priests or Levites. It names the simple, who get prudence, and the young, who get knowledge and discretion. That's the whole guest list for this one. I'd say that leaves the door pretty wide open for the rest of us.

Not quite, friend. Verse 5 says, “…let the wise listen and gain instruction, and the discerning acquire wise counsel” The wise are right there in the sentence, and they're told to listen. No skipping allowed, even for the experts. Even I keep reading my own recipes.

That's right. Verse 5 says, “…let the wise listen and gain instruction, and the discerning acquire wise counsel” The wise aren't excused from the book, they're invited into it. They're the ones told to listen. Being wise just means you keep listening.

Verse 7 says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge…” That's the starting line, baker, before any single proverb gets going. Knowledge begins right there. You've got a solid first layer now.

The king does show up in the very first verse, since Solomon, David's son, is called king of Israel. But verse 7 doesn't start knowledge with his favor. It says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge…” Knowledge begins there, friend.

Good instinct to think of advice from people who've been around, friend. But verse 7 gives a different starting point: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge…” That's where knowledge begins. Everything else comes after it.

Yes, it's all in one verse. Right after naming where knowledge begins, verse 7 goes on, “…but fools despise wisdom and discipline.” The word but sets the two sides by side. The beginning of knowledge on one side, and what fools despise on the other. Short verse, big contrast.

It really is there, baker. Verse 7 doesn't stop after the fear of the LORD. It keeps going: “…but fools despise wisdom and discipline.” Same verse, same breath. It's an easy one to miss, and I'd double check too.

Verse 8 says, “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.” So the father's instruction and the mother's teaching are both named in the same verse. The son is told to listen to the one and not forsake the other.

A brother never shows up in verse 8. It says, “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.” So it's mom's teaching he's told to hold onto. No brothers on this one, friend.

The elders aren't named in verse 8. The voice says, “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.” It stays right at home, with his father and his mother. That's the whole family circle in this verse.

Verse 9 says, “For they are a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck.” One goes on the head and one goes around the neck. The voice reaches for things a person wears, baker. Nothing in this verse is armor.

Armor is a fun guess, but this verse is more of a jewelry counter. It says the teaching is “…a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck.” A garland sits on the head and a pendant hangs at the neck. No breastplate in sight, friend.

Those aren't in verse 9, friend. The voice says the teaching is “…a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck.” So it's a garland for the head and a pendant for the neck. Nobody's holding anything in this picture.

Verse 10 says it plainly: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not yield to them.” Entice means they'll try to pull him in. The instruction is to not yield. It's a short sentence, and the voice doesn't dress it up.
It's the other way around, baker. Verse 10 says, “My son, if sinners entice you, do not yield to them.” He isn't told to give in. He's told not to yield.

Verse 11 has the sinners saying, “…let us ambush the innocent without cause…” The people they're after have done nothing to deserve it. I think this one hurts to read. The sinners say it right out loud in their pitch.

The sinners don't claim that, friend. Verse 11 has them say, “…let us ambush the innocent without cause…” So the people they target are innocent, and they plan it without cause. I think this is a heavy line.

Verse 11 doesn't call the targets foolish. The sinners say, “…let us ambush the innocent without cause…” Innocent is the word, and without cause is how the voice says it. I think it's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it simple.

In verse 13 the sinners say, “We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder.” Notice it's a pitch, baker. Right alongside the goods, they talk about lying in wait for blood in verse 11. Plunder is the prize they're offering.
Honor isn't in their pitch, friend. Verse 13 has them say, “We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder.” The promise is goods and plunder. Honor never comes up.
Peace is a nice thing to promise, but it's not in this pitch. Verse 13 has the sinners say, “we will fill our houses with plunder.” Plunder is what they're selling. Peace never comes up.

Not so, baker. Verse 15 goes further than skipping the ambush: “…do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path.” It isn't just the ambush. He's told to stay off the road and off their path altogether. Not one step.

That's right. Verse 15 says, “…do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path.” The instruction covers walking with them at all, not only the ambush itself. The voice says it twice in one verse, once as the road and once as the path.

Verse 16 gives the reason: “For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood.” It's about where they're headed and how fast they move. That's why the son is told not to set foot on their path. The path leads where their feet are running.
Verse 16 doesn't say that, friend. It says, “For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood.” The reason given is evil and shedding blood. The king doesn't come up.

The Sabbath doesn't show up in this passage at all. Verse 16 gives the reason: “For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood.” That's what the son is told to stay away from. It's all about where their feet are headed.

That's the twist, baker. Verse 18 says, “But they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives.” Back in verse 17 comes the line about spreading the net where any bird can see it. Then verse 18 says the sinners are lying in wait for their own blood. The ambush they talked about is aimed at their own lives.

The king isn't in this part, friend. Verse 18 says, “But they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives.” The voice turns the whole plan back on the sinners themselves. That's the twist.

Families aren't named in verse 18. The voice says, “But they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives.” Their own blood, their own lives. The ambush they planned for somebody else is aimed at them.

Verse 19 says, “Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors.” Remember the plunder and the shared purse from their pitch? The verse says the fate belongs to all who are greedy. Their unjust gain takes the lives of those who hold it.

Lazy isn't the word in verse 19. It says, “Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors.” Greedy is who the verse names. These sinners were chasing plunder, and that's the greed the voice is pointing at.

Pride isn't named in verse 19, baker. It says, “Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors.” The word is greedy. That ties right back to the plunder in their pitch.
